theme: Into your hands I commit my spirit
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 31:1-18. This is a psalm of trust in deep distress. Verse 5 is the one Jesus prayed on the cross, and you will meet it again in Luke 23.
settingTheScene: Psalm 31 is a psalm of David written when he was in danger, grieving, and slandered. It moves back and forth between trust and complaint, a mark of honest prayer. The first eighteen verses cover the prayer for refuge, the description of suffering, and the declaration, “My times are in your hand.” The rest of the psalm (vv. 19 to 24) comes in a few days.
observation: “In you, O LORD, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame; in your righteousness deliver me!” (v. 1).
“Be to me a rock of refuge, a strong fortress to save me!” (v. 2).
“For you are my rock and my fortress” (v. 3).
“Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God” (v. 5).
“Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am in distress” (v. 9).
“For my life is spent with sorrow, and my years with sighing” (v. 10).
“But I trust in you, O LORD; I say, You are my God” (v. 14).
interpretation:
The psalm starts with a refuge. David has run to the LORD, and he asks to be delivered. He uses the image of a rock and a fortress, and asks the LORD to lead and guide him “for your name’s sake.” Whatever happens, God’s own honor is tied to his people.

Verse 5 is the center: “Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God.” This was a prayer a pious Jew might say at bedtime. It means, “I place my life in your keeping.” Jesus will pray it on the cross, with one change: he begins with “Father.” The prayer David prayed in danger is the prayer Jesus prayed in death, and it has been the prayer of many Christians in their last moments.

Then David describes his suffering. He is in distress. His eye, soul, and body waste away with grief. His strength fails because of his iniquity, and his bones waste away. He has become a reproach to his adversaries and an object of dread to his neighbors. People who see him flee from him. He is forgotten like one who is dead, a broken vessel. He hears the whispering of many, terror on every side, as they scheme to take his life.

And yet: “But I trust in you, O LORD; I say, You are my God.” The word “but” turns the psalm. In the middle of terror he declares, “My times are in your hand.” All of life’s seasons, the good and the bad, are in God’s hand. No enemy can reach beyond it. So he asks God to make his face shine on him and to save him in his steadfast love.

This is the heart of faith. It does not deny the pain, and it does not say the pain is small. It says that the pain is held by a hand that is good.
connection: Luke 23:46 has Jesus praying verse 5 on the cross. Acts 7:59 has Stephen praying a similar prayer at his death. Jonah 2:8 and Psalm 71:1-3 parallel the refuge language. Psalm 22 is also a psalm of suffering and trust. Romans 8:28 says God works all things together for good. 1 Peter 4:19 says to entrust your souls to a faithful Creator. 1 Peter 5:7 says to cast all your anxieties on him.
application:
Pray verse 5 tonight before you sleep, and let it become a habit.

Write “My times are in your hand” on a card and place it where you will see it.

Name a season of your life that feels out of control and entrust it to God.
prayerPrompts: Commit your spirit into God’s hand, as Jesus did.
Tell him what you need as your refuge.
